content:
Quick answer: Pacing means doing a steady, planned amount of activity each day, rather than a lot on good days and very little on bad ones. Find your baseline, the amount you can manage even on a bad day, break tasks into chunks with short rests, then increase gradually. It helps reduce flares of pain and fatigue caused by boom and bust.

"I do too much on a good day, then pay for it for the rest of the week." If that sounds familiar, pacing is for you. Pacing is one of the most useful self-management skills for living with arthritis pain and fatigue, and it is widely taught by NHS physiotherapists, occupational therapists and pain services. It is not about doing less forever. It is about doing a steady, sustainable amount so you can gradually do more, with fewer crashes. This guide shows you how, step by step, with worked examples.

What pacing is, and what it is not

Pacing is: planning your activity so you do a similar amount each day, breaking tasks into manageable chunks, taking short rests before you need them, and building up gradually over time.

Pacing is not: resting all the time, giving up things you enjoy, or only doing things when pain is low. Too much rest leads to stiffness, weakness and lower fitness, which make everyday tasks harder.

NICE's guideline on osteoarthritis (NG226) puts exercise and staying active at the centre of treatment, and NICE's chronic pain guideline (NG193) recommends supervised group exercise programmes for people with chronic primary pain. Pacing is what makes regular activity possible when pain and fatigue are unpredictable.

The boom-and-bust cycle

Many people with arthritis fall into this pattern without realising:

  1. You have a good day and try to catch up on everything: cleaning, shopping, gardening.
  2. Pain and fatigue rise later that day or the next.
  3. You rest for several days to recover.
  4. Jobs pile up and you lose fitness.
  5. When you feel better, you overdo it again to catch up.

Over time, the "bust" periods can get longer and the "boom" days shorter. Pacing breaks the cycle by smoothing out the peaks and troughs.

Step 1: notice your patterns

For a week, keep a simple activity diary. Note what you did, for how long, and your pain and energy scores (0 to 10) morning, afternoon and evening. Look for:

  • Activities that reliably lead to more pain or fatigue later
  • How long after an activity the pain comes on, which is often hours later or the next day
  • Busy days followed by crash days
  • Times of day when you have most energy

Our pain tracking journal has a table you can use.

Step 2: find your baseline

Your baseline is the amount of an activity you can do on a bad day as well as a good day, without a significant flare afterwards. To work it out:

  1. Choose an activity, for example walking, standing to cook, or using a computer.
  2. Note how long you can do it on a few different days before pain or fatigue rises noticeably.
  3. Take an average, then reduce it a little, often by around a fifth, to give a comfortable starting point.

Example: on different days you managed to stand and cook for 25, 15 and 20 minutes before your back and knees hurt. The average is 20 minutes. Your baseline might be around 15 minutes.

It feels frustrating to start lower than you know you can do on a good day. That is the point: a baseline you can manage every day lets you build up without crashing.

Step 3: break tasks into chunks

Once you know your baselines, split bigger tasks so no single chunk goes over them:

  • Cleaning: one room a day, rather than the whole house on Saturday.
  • Cooking: prepare vegetables sitting down in the morning, cook in the evening.
  • Shopping: two small shops instead of one big one, or an online delivery.
  • Gardening: 15 minutes of weeding, a rest, then 15 minutes of something different.
  • Work: change task or position every 30 minutes or so.

Step 4: plan rests before you need them

Rest breaks work best when they are short, planned and taken before pain or tiredness builds, not after you have pushed through.

  • Use a timer on your phone or cooker to remind you to stop.
  • Take a 5- to 10-minute break between chunks.
  • Make the break genuinely restful: sit down, stretch gently, breathe slowly or have a drink.
  • For fatigue, two or three longer planned rests in the day can help. See our energy management guide.

Step 5: plan your day and week

  • Spread heavy tasks across the week rather than bunching them.
  • Alternate heavy and light tasks, sitting and standing, physical and mental activities.
  • Use your best time of day for the most important or demanding tasks.
  • Plan around events. Before a big day such as a wedding or a trip, do less the day before and plan a quieter day after.
  • Prioritise. Ask: does this need doing today? Does it need doing by me? Could it be done more easily?

A simple way to plan is the "4 Ps" many therapists use: Prioritise, Plan, Pace and Position (use good posture and positions that put less strain on joints).

Step 6: build up gradually

Once your baseline feels manageable for about a week, increase it by a small amount, often suggested as around 10 per cent to a fifth. For example, from 15 minutes of cooking to 17 minutes, or from 10 minutes of walking to 11 or 12.

  • Keep the new level for several days to a week before increasing again.
  • Increase one activity at a time.
  • If you have a flare, drop back to an earlier level until it settles, then build up again.
  • Write your progress down. It is easy to forget how far you have come.

Worked examples

Walking

Baseline: 8 minutes on a flat route without a pain spike later. Week 1: walk 8 minutes daily. Week 2: 9 minutes. Week 3: 10 minutes. Continue adding a minute or two a week. If a longer walk flares your knee, go back a step. Our guide to walking with arthritis has a full plan.

Housework

Instead of a two-hour clean on Saturday that leaves you exhausted on Sunday and Monday, do 20 minutes each morning with a 10-minute rest between tasks. Sit to iron, use a long-handled duster and a lightweight vacuum, and leave heavy tasks for someone else where possible. See our guide to joint protection.

Computer work

Baseline: 30 minutes before your neck and hands ache. Set a timer for 25 minutes, then stand, stretch and move for 3 to 5 minutes. Alternate typing with phone calls or reading.

A day out

Plan the route and parking, include sit-down breaks every hour, take a folding stick seat if helpful, and keep the next day quiet. Book assistance at stations or attractions if you need it.

Pacing thinking, feelings and social energy

Pacing is not only about physical tasks. Concentrating, dealing with paperwork, difficult conversations, busy social events and worry all use energy, and can leave you as drained as housework.

  • Spread mental tasks. Do forms, emails or bill paying in short sessions, ideally at your best time of day.
  • Mix types of activity. Follow a mentally demanding task with something physical and gentle, or a rest, rather than another demanding task.
  • Plan social time. Seeing people is important, but long or noisy events can be tiring. Agree a time to leave, find a quieter spot to sit, or meet for a shorter coffee instead of a long meal.
  • Notice stress. Stressful periods often use up more energy than you expect. Lower your physical baselines a little during them.
  • Use relaxation as a planned rest. Slow breathing or a short relaxation exercise can make a break more restorative.

Common pacing problems and fixes

ProblemTry
"I feel fine, so I keep going."Use a timer and stop at your planned time, even on good days. Good days are when boom and bust starts.
"I lose track of time."Phone alarms, kitchen timers or a smartwatch reminder.
"Other people expect me to do more."Explain pacing to family, friends and your employer. Share this page if it helps.
"I feel guilty resting."Rest is part of the plan, like taking medicine. It helps you do more over the week.
"My baseline is so low it is depressing."Focus on the trend over weeks. Small, steady increases add up.
"Pain still varies even when I pace."That is normal. Pacing reduces big swings but does not remove all variation.

Pacing with different types of arthritis

  • Osteoarthritis: pain often follows load, so pacing standing, walking and lifting is especially useful, alongside strengthening exercises.
  • Inflammatory arthritis: fatigue is often a big factor. Pacing helps, but persistent fatigue with joint swelling may mean the disease is active, so talk to your rheumatology team.
  • Fibromyalgia alongside arthritis: pacing is a core strategy, combined with gradual activity and good sleep.
  • During a flare: drop baselines temporarily and follow your flare-up plan.

Getting help with pacing

Physiotherapists and occupational therapists can help you set baselines and plan activity. The NHS explains that occupational therapy helps people manage daily activities, and you can often be referred by your GP or rheumatology team. Some areas have NHS pain management programmes or self-management courses for long-term conditions. Ask your GP what is available locally.

When to get medical help

  • See your GP if pain or fatigue is getting worse despite pacing, if you are struggling to manage everyday tasks, or if you have new joint swelling or long morning stiffness.
  • Contact your rheumatology team if you have inflammatory arthritis and more joints are swelling or fatigue is increasing.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E for a suddenly hot, red, swollen joint with fever or feeling unwell.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or signs of a stroke.
  • Talk to your GP if pain is affecting your mood. In England, you can self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies.

What does pacing mean for arthritis?

Pacing means doing a steady, planned amount of activity each day, breaking tasks into chunks with short rests, and building up gradually. It helps avoid the boom-and-bust pattern of overdoing it on good days and crashing afterwards.

How do I work out my baseline?

Note how long you can do an activity on several different days before pain or fatigue rises noticeably, take the average, then reduce it a little. That is a level you should be able to manage even on a bad day without a flare afterwards.

How quickly should I increase activity when pacing?

Slowly. A common approach is to increase by around 10 per cent to a fifth once your current level feels manageable for about a week. Increase one activity at a time, and drop back if you flare.

Is pacing the same as resting more?

No. Pacing includes planned rests, but the aim is to stay active and gradually do more. Too much rest reduces fitness and strength and can make pain and fatigue worse over time.

What should I do on a good day?

Stick broadly to your plan. It is tempting to catch up on everything, but good days are when boom and bust usually starts. You can add a small, planned extra activity, but keep your rests.

Can pacing help with arthritis fatigue as well as pain?

Yes. Pacing is one of the main self-management approaches for fatigue, alongside planned rest, good sleep and gradual activity. If fatigue is severe or getting worse, see your GP to check for treatable causes.
